bullets: **AO1 = 8 marks**: a critical, personal, well-supported response; a clear argument; apt quotations.
**AO2 = 12 marks**: analysis of language, form and structure and their effects, with precise terminology.
Suggested time: about **40–45 minutes** (10 reading and annotating, 30–35 writing). Check your school’s advice for timing across the whole paper.
Comparison is essential throughout.
core.p: You read two unseen poems on a shared theme and answer one comparison question, e.g. ‘Compare the ways the writers present ideas about…’. There is **no AO3** in Section C: context is not rewarded, so do not spend time guessing it.

bullets: **Read each poem twice**: first for meaning (what happens? who speaks? what changes?), then for method.
**Find the turn**: where does the tone or focus shift? Turns are gold for structure marks.
**Annotate** 4–5 moments per poem: title, opening, a key image, the turn, the ending; plus one form feature (stanzas, rhyme, rhythm, line length).
**Write a thesis** comparing the poets’ attitudes to the theme.
**Write 3–4 comparative paragraphs**: one on the central contrast, one on imagery/language, one on form and structure, one on endings.
**Tentative language** for interpretations: ‘perhaps’, ‘this could suggest’, ‘alternatively’.

callouts.p: Every poem has a shape: something changes between the beginning and end. Name that change for each poem, and you have your structure paragraph.

core.h: The method: read, annotate, plan, write

bullets: Only a man harrowing clods
In a slow silent walk
With an old horse that stumbles and nods
Half asleep as they stalk.
Only thin smoke without flame
From the heaps of couch-grass;
Yet this will go onward the same
Though Dynasties pass.
Yonder a maid and her wight
Come whispering by:
War's annals will cloud into night
Ere their story die.
core.h: The model poems: poem 1 (both are out of copyright)
core.p: **Poem 1: In Time of ‘The Breaking of Nations’ (Thomas Hardy, 1916)**

bullets: The flowers left thick at nightfall in the wood
This Eastertide call into mind the men,
Now far from home, who, with their sweethearts, should
Have gathered them and will do never again.

callouts.p: harrowing clods = breaking up lumps of earth before sowing; couch-grass = a weed burned in heaps; wight = (old word) man, here a lover; annals = historical records; Eastertide = the Easter season.

plan: Form and structure: three slow stanzas vs one sentence
essays.q: Compare the ways the writers present ideas about war and everyday life in In Time of ‘The Breaking of Nations’ and In Memoriam (Easter, 1915).
essays.t: Model answer: Section C unseen comparison
essays.text:
Both poets write about the First World War almost without mentioning fighting, turning instead to the quiet rhythms of country life; however, Hardy finds consolation in the idea that ordinary life will outlast war, whereas Thomas suggests that war has already broken that life by removing the men who should be living it.

Hardy’s poem presents everyday life as permanent. The repeated opening word ‘Only’ seems to belittle the scenes, ‘Only a man harrowing clods’, ‘Only thin smoke without flame’, yet the repetition gradually builds a sense of quiet endurance. The man, the old horse that ‘stumbles and nods’ and the heaps of burning couch-grass are humble, unchanging images of farming, and the slow alliteration of ‘slow silent walk’ gives the stanza an unhurried, almost timeless pace. The turn comes with ‘Yet this will go onward the same / Though Dynasties pass’: the capitalised ‘Dynasties’, which stands for kings, empires and the war they wage, is dwarfed by the smallest acts of daily work. Thomas also focuses on rural life, but in his poem it is marked by absence. The ‘flowers left thick at nightfall in the wood’ are beautiful, yet the adjective ‘left’ suggests they are uncollected, and their abundance becomes a sign of the men who are missing. Where Hardy’s countryside proves that life continues, Thomas’s countryside reminds the speaker of who is gone.

The poets’ treatment of love sharpens this difference. Hardy’s final stanza introduces ‘a maid and her wight’ who ‘Come whispering by’; the archaic word ‘wight’ and the soft sibilance create an intimate, almost fairy-tale tone. Love here is fragile but enduring. Thomas also imagines young lovers, men gathering flowers ‘with their sweethearts’, but only in the conditional: they ‘should / Have gathered them’. The modal verb ‘should’ marks what ought to have happened, and the line break after it creates a painful pause, as if the speaker cannot bear to finish the thought. Hardy’s lovers are present and whispering; Thomas’s are a vision of what war has prevented.

The forms reinforce these attitudes. Hardy uses three short quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme and short lines, so the poem moves slowly and steadily, like the farmer and his horse; its regularity reflects his belief in continuity. Thomas compresses his whole poem into one four-line sentence. Its long, enjambed lines run on through the commas of ‘Now far from home, who, with their sweethearts, should’, delaying the main point, and the poem is so brief that it feels like an epitaph or an inscription, which fits its title, In Memoriam. The structure of a single sentence gives the final words enormous weight.

The endings complete each poet’s argument. Hardy ends with a confident prophecy: ‘War’s annals will cloud into night / Ere their story die’. The metaphor of history ‘clouding into night’ suggests that the official records of war will fade before the private story of love does, a consoling idea in 1916. Thomas’s ending is the opposite of consolation: the men ‘will do never again’. The unusual word order places ‘never’ just before ‘again’, so the last words land with finality, and the absence of any comfort or explanation makes the grief more powerful through restraint. Ultimately, Hardy’s poem reassures the reader that ordinary life is stronger than war, whereas Thomas’s poem quietly insists that, for the men who did not come home, ordinary life has already ended.
essays.thesis: Both poets write about the First World War almost without mentioning fighting, turning instead to the quiet rhythms of rural life; but Hardy finds consolation in the idea that ordinary life will outlast war, whereas Thomas shows that war has already broken that life by removing the men who should be living it.
why: **AO1 (8)**: a clear, personal, critical argument with a thesis sustained to the end; quotations embedded and apt.

**AO2 (12)**: repetition, alliteration, capitalisation, adjectives, archaic diction, sibilance, modal verb, line break, rhyme scheme, stanza form, enjambment, single-sentence structure, metaphor, word order.
**No AO3**: context (the war) is used only to understand meaning, not as a separate point.

model: Hardy: three stanzas, turn at ‘Yet’, prophetic ending
Thomas: one sentence, delayed main clause, final ‘never again’
exam.q: Practice: compare how the writers present loss in these two poems, focusing only on structure (one paragraph, 12 minutes).
exam.tip: Structure = shape, turn and ending. Always.

mistakes.r: Section C has no AO3; use what the poems say.
mistakes.w: Writing about context (‘In WW1 lots of people died’).
Analysing one poem fully, then the other.

mistakes.r: Form and structure are part of AO2: comment on stanzas, rhyme, line length, turns and endings.
Use context in the poem to infer meaning; glossaries are often given.

summary: Section C of Edexcel Paper 2 gives you two poems you have never seen and asks you to compare them for 20 marks: 8 for AO1 (critical, informed personal response with references) and 12 for AO2 (language, form, structure); this note gives a step-by-step method and a full model answer on two out-of-copyright poems.

terms.d: A verb expressing possibility or obligation (should, could, will).
A short text in memory of the dead, often on a gravestone.
Phrases like ‘perhaps’ or ‘this could suggest’ that present an interpretation thoughtfully.
